reason: The sources provide 15 distinct claims supported by at least two sites, confirming the myth-busting premise that aerodynamic forces, not an explosion, destroyed the shuttle.
story: On January 28, 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger disintegrated 73 seconds into its 10th mission. Contrary to popular belief, the orbiter did not explode; it was torn apart by aerodynamic forces. The disaster began when record-low temperatures stiffened rubber O-ring seals in the right rocket booster. These failed seals allowed hot gases to burn through the external fuel tank, causing it to collapse. This structural failure forced the shuttle stack into an abnormal direction while traveling at nearly twice the speed of sound. The resulting supersonic wind shear was too intense for the airframe to withstand, shredding the orbiter. The crew cabin remained largely intact during the breakup. Evidence from activated emergency air packs suggests at least some of the seven crew members were conscious during their two-and-a-half-minute fall to the ocean. Despite urgent warnings from engineers about the cold, NASA managers had pushed for launch. Today, the shuttle's wreckage is buried in missile silos at Cape Canaveral.
angle: The Space Shuttle Challenger did not actually explode; it was literally torn apart by supersonic wind shear after a $700 rubber seal failed in the cold.

claims.claim: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff on mission STS-51-L.
The orbiter was torn apart by aerodynamic forces rather than a technical explosion.
The primary cause was the failure of O-ring seals in the right solid rocket booster.
Record-low temperatures on the morning of the launch caused the rubber O-rings to stiffen.
Hot pressurized gas leaked through the booster joint and burned into the external propellant tank.
The crew cabin separated in one piece from the rest of the orbiter during the breakup.
All seven crew members were killed, including teacher Christa McAuliffe.
NASA managers disregarded warnings from engineers about launching in low temperatures.
NASA official Lawrence Mulloy pressured engineers by asking if they wanted him to wait until April to launch.
The Rogers Commission was formed by President Reagan to investigate the disaster.
Most of the recovered non-organic debris from Challenger is buried in retired missile silos at Cape Canaveral.

disputed: The existence of a recording of the crew panicking during the fall is considered a fabrication and no such recording exists.
Claims that the White House pressured NASA to launch for the State of the Union address were investigated and found to be unsupported.
The exact cause and timing of the crew's deaths remain unknown as the ocean impact masked evidence of damage.
